B.I.G Mule: The Teacher, Artist and Musician Behind “Chikasalanga”

News updates, trivia, entertainment,sport, myths,nostalgia, politics, history, celebrity gossip and many more.

Actual Article Body:
There are musicians you meet on a stage, musicians you discover through a song, and then there are musicians whose stories become intertwined with your own journey. For me, B.I.G Mule belongs to the third category.

Long before our music found its way into a recording studio, our paths crossed in the world of education. We were young men finding our way, studying, teaching, thinking about the future and, somewhere in between, discovering that music was refusing to leave us alone.

His name is Mulenga Pule, but to those who know him through music, he is B.I.G Mule : a teacher by profession, painter, musician, lover of history, geography, mathematics and art, and a strong Rastafari believer whose worldview often stretches beyond the ordinary.

Today, he is based in Mpika, but his story remains deeply connected to Kabwe, a city that has produced generations of musicians, artists and cultural storytellers.

B.I.G Mule began making his presence felt on the Zambian music scene following the release of “Chikasalanga” in 2013.

For an emerging musician, releasing a song is one thing. Building a musical identity around that song is another. B.I.G Mule's journey gradually opened doors to collaborations with names such as hardcore rapper Muzo, Ron Kay of Zedpride, Jerry Fingers and other artists.

But perhaps one of the most interesting aspects of his musical history is that his journey did not exist in isolation.

During his early prime, B.I.G Mule had the opportunity to work with one of Kabwe's legendary artist Emmy roots of the late 1990s and early 2000s. A period when Zambian music was developing its own distinct sound and artists from provincial towns were contributing to the country's growing musical identity.

That connection placed B.I.G Mule within a much bigger story: the passing of musical knowledge from one generation to another.

I first crossed paths with B.I.G Mule in 2014, when I was doing my teaching practice at Lukanga Primary School.

At the time, he was studying at Parglory University, while I was studying at Immaculata Teachers College.

We were both students preparing for professional lives in education. But beneath the books, assignments and teaching practice were two people carrying another passion "music".

As our friendship grew, we began introducing each other to our music.

That exchange became important to my own musical journey because B.I.G Mule later introduced me to the humble Ron Kay from Zedpride. What initially looked like an ordinary friendship between two aspiring teachers eventually became a bridge connecting musicians, ideas and creative possibilities.

This is one of the beautiful things about creative communities. Sometimes the most important collaborations do not begin with contracts, managers or record labels. They begin with friendship.

Eventually, B.I.G Mule and I found ourselves doing what musicians naturally do when ideas begin to connect: we recorded music together.

The result was “Take Me Away,” a collaboration between B.I.G Mule and myself.

The record was produced by Uncle Remo, one of Kabwe's respected and legendary producers, at TQRV.

For me, the song represents more than another entry in a catalogue of recordings. It carries a piece of a particular period in our lives the friendships, the musical experimentation, the people we met and the creative environment that surrounded us.

Songs can become time capsules.

Years later, you can hear a familiar voice, a particular beat or a line from an old recording and suddenly find yourself transported back to a place you thought you had forgotten.

“Take Me Away” is one of those records for me.

What makes B.I.G Mule interesting is that music is only one part of his identity.

He is a teacher, and perhaps that helps explain his fascination with subjects such as history, geography and mathematics. He is also a painter, giving him another language through which to interpret the world.
